title: Fast preparation and recycling method for colloidal probe cantilevers in hydrophobic mapping applications
author: Babel, Rudolph
materials: This section contains the used materials and methods including chemicals, probes, probe preparation and attachment procedures as well as the cantilever recycling procedure. As a general, remark the authors suggest for each surface described and handled in the procedure the use of powder free gloves.

steps.title: Clean SiO2 colloidal spheres
steps.instruction: Disperse 19.59 µm (±0.69 µm) SiO₂ spheres in ROTISOLV® HPLC‑grade ethanol and place in an ultrasonic bath for 10 min; repeat sedimentation, ethanol removal and re‑addition ten times.

steps.title: Prepare planar quartz reference
steps.instruction: Embed a clear quartz crystal in epoxy resin, machine‑polish to 0.3 nm Ra / 0.5 nm Rq roughness. For each contact‑angle test, re‑polish with 0.04 µm amorphous SiO₂ dispersion on an OP‑Chem polishing cloth for 1 min, sonicate 5 min in DI water, rinse with ethanol, wipe with a lint‑free cloth, sonicate another 5 min in DI water, dry with compressed air, and plasma‑clean in O₂ for 10 min.

steps.title: Deposit particles on clean slide
steps.instruction: Place the cleaned SiO₂ spheres onto a polished and cleaned microscope slide (or cover slip) prepared as in the previous step to avoid contaminant transfer.

steps.title: Apply UV‑curable glue to cantilever
steps.instruction: Deposit Ber‑Fix® UV Gel onto a cover slip, spread a thin layer with a second cover slip, then gently bring the cantilever tip into contact with the glue film using the AFM drives to coat the lower end. If excess glue appears, remove it with acetone or ethanol or by brief O₂ plasma cleaning.

steps.title: Attach particle to glue‑coated cantilever
steps.instruction: Under an optical microscope, move the AFM‑controlled cantilever toward a single SiO₂ sphere on the slide and bring the tip into contact to bond the particle to the glue layer.

steps.title: Cure glue and plasma clean
steps.instruction: Place the cantilever (still on the slide) beneath a 395 nm UV‑LED and irradiate for 90 s to cure the glue, then perform O₂ plasma cleaning for 10 min to activate the surface without compromising adhesive strength.

steps.title: Pre‑functionalization plasma cleaning
steps.instruction: Subject the glued probe to an additional O₂ plasma cleaning for 10 min to further clean and activate the surface before silane deposition.

steps.title: Silane functionalization of probe
steps.instruction: In a drying cabinet set to 115 °C, place the cantilever in a Petri dish containing a reagent reservoir. Add 50 µL of DYNASYLAN® F8261 silane to the reservoir, cover with a second Petri dish (not airtight), and incubate for 2 h. After silane evaporation, add 100 µL deionized water to the reservoir and continue curing for 20 min. Total functionalization time is 140 min.

steps.title: Final plasma activation
steps.instruction: After silane curing, perform a final O₂ plasma cleaning for 10 min to ensure surface activation for hydrophobic measurements.

steps.title: Verify silane layer by contact angle
steps.instruction: Measure the water contact angle on a quartz crystal (prepared as in step 2) before functionalization and after each functionalization time point (0–120 min) using a DataPhysics OCA 50, applying 0.3 µL DI water in a saturated environment.

steps.title: Recycle cantilever – glue removal
steps.instruction: Place the used cantilever in O₂ plasma and clean for a duration sufficient to reduce glue mass (monitor via resonance frequency if desired); a typical initial 10 min removes ~20 % of the glue.

steps.title: Detach particle and final cleaning
steps.instruction: After plasma cleaning, remove the SiO₂ particle with water, ethanol, acetone, or micromanipulation; then perform a final O₂ plasma cleaning to eliminate residual glue before attaching a fresh particle.

steps.title: Optional long‑term plasma aging test
steps.instruction: Treat pristine cantilevers in O₂ plasma for 10 h, periodically measuring resonance frequency to assess coating stability (average frequency change observed 0.09 %).

description: Colloidal probe atomic force microscopy (CP-AFM) was first reported by [1,2] and is nowadays used in multiple applications in various fields of research. One possible application are adhesive force mappings on a variety of samples including biological [[3], [4], [5]], mineral [6,7], ceramic [[8], [9], [10]] or wooden samples [3,11]. Beside possible sources of contamination during storing in ambient conditions as summarized by [12], the main source of colloidal probe contamination in an adhesive force mapping application on mineral surfaces experienced by the authors are inorganic particulate contaminations [13], as given in Fig. 1. The contaminations originate from the sample preparation procedure either by constituents of the polishing suspension for the substrate, like abrasives and additives or the minerals themselves. In literature there are no reports on probe durability, reproducibility between different probes and or cantilevers in adhesion mapping applications. Wallqvist et al. reported on investigations with about 50 points [14] to 560 points [15] and an example with an extensive mapping (400 points) was reported by Xie et al. [16] with no comment on probe durability or reproducibility of measurements.Fig. 1Scanning electron microscope (SEM) image of a colloidal probe prepared with this protocol after surface contamination during scanning. Fixating glue is not present on the upper half of the sphere.Fig. 1 As the mechanical scrubbing procedure proposed by [12] could not be successfully applied and high loads possibly damage the functionalization of the colloid, we propose a fast probe preparation procedure for recyclable colloidal probe cantilevers. This includes the demonstration of a fast surface modification and probe removal method without the aid of solvents or acids as they possibly contain and transport contaminants, which are potentially problematic for the reflex coating of the cantilever.
